segments.text: Lightning hits a park ranger in the mountains of Virginia. He lives. Then it hits him again. And again. Seven times, over thirty-five years. And he survives every one.
No chance. Not seven. Let's go look.

His name is Roy Sullivan. Born in Virginia in {1912|nineteen twelve}. He is a ranger in Shenandoah National Park, up in the Blue Ridge Mountains. It is a job that keeps a man outdoors, on high ground, in all weather.
April, {1942|nineteen forty-two}. A storm comes over the ridge, and Roy Sullivan, thirty years old, shelters in a fire lookout tower. It is new. By the usual account, it has no lightning rod yet.
The tower is hit, and it catches fire. He runs for it. A few steps from the tower, the bolt finds him. It burns a line down his right leg, takes a toenail, and leaves a hole in his shoe.
And then, nothing. For twenty-seven years, the sky leaves him alone. One strike. Most people would call that their share.

July, {1969|nineteen sixty-nine}. He is driving his truck on a mountain road. A closed vehicle is where you are supposed to be safe. The account is that the bolt comes off the trees and in at the open window. It knocks him out cold, and takes his eyebrows.
One year later, he is standing in his own front yard. It sears his left shoulder.
April, {1972|nineteen seventy-two}. He is indoors this time, inside a ranger station. It makes no difference. His hair catches fire.
That is four. After that, he keeps a can of water in his truck. I thought that was a joke. It isn't.
August, {1973|nineteen seventy-three}. He is out on patrol, standing by the truck. His hair burns again, and his legs are seared. And he uses the can.
People have names for him. The Human Lightning Rod. The Spark Ranger.
And it is said that people start keeping their distance when the sky turns dark. I would laugh. He didn't. It is a lonely thing, to be the man nobody stands next to.
It doesn't even stay with him. His wife is hit once, hanging out washing in their back yard. He is right there, helping her. That time, it misses him.
June, {1976|nineteen seventy-six}. Number six. An injured ankle, and his hair, again.

June, {1977|nineteen seventy-seven}. Thirty-five years after the tower. He is sixty-five, and he is fishing. It comes down on him one more time. His chest and his stomach are burned, and he is taken to hospital.

Now, the arithmetic. Guinness puts the chance of being struck even once, in a long lifetime, at about one in ten thousand. He manages seven. Then again, most people don't spend their working lives on a mountain ridge.

I went looking for the catch. The strikes were put on record by the park's superintendent, who, it has to be said, was not standing next to him at the time. But Guinness lists all seven, with the date and the damage.
Seven strikes. Seven times, he gets up. Nobody on record has survived more.
Two of his ranger hats, with the crowns scorched, went on display in Guinness exhibit halls.
He died in {1983|nineteen eighty-three}. He was seventy-one. In those last six years, the lightning never came back.

I came to prove nobody takes seven. He did. And after every one, he got back up. One piece of advice, from a crow who has now watched it seven times: when you hear thunder, go indoors. I was wrong. Case closed.
